screens.title: Why Custom Rules?
screens.narratorSegment: SonarQube comes packed with a vast array of built-in rules and allows for extensive customization through Quality Profiles. However, even with these powerful features, there will inevitably be situations where your organization has very specific coding standards, unique architectural patterns, or domain-specific best practices that simply aren't covered by the default rule set. Imagine a scenario where your company mandates a particular way of handling logging or a specific design pattern for service interfaces. These are precisely the gaps that custom rules are designed to fill. They empower you to extend SonarQube's analysis capabilities, ensuring that your code quality checks are perfectly aligned with your internal guidelines. Without custom rules, you might miss critical violations of your unique standards, leading to inconsistencies and potential technical debt that SonarQube would otherwise help prevent. This extensibility is what makes SonarQube truly adaptable to any development environment. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of how SonarQube performs static analysis lies a fundamental concept: the Abstract Syntax Tree, or AST. Think of an AST as a hierarchical, tree-like representation of your source code, but stripped of all the syntactic details that aren't essential for understanding its structure. For example, when you write an 'if' statement, a 'for' loop, a method declaration, or a variable assignment in your code, each of these constructs is represented as a distinct node within the AST. SonarQube's powerful rules engine then traverses this tree, systematically examining each node and its relationships to others, searching for specific patterns or anti-patterns that indicate potential code quality issues or vulnerabilities. When you develop a custom rule, you are essentially writing your own code that also navigates this very same AST, allowing you to pinpoint and flag your organization's unique patterns. Understanding the AST is crucial because it's the canvas on which all SonarQube's analysis, both built-in and custom, is painted. A common misconception is that SonarQube analyzes raw text; instead, it works with this structured, semantic representation. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5›Chapter 5.2›Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)

Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)

The core data structure for SonarQube's static analysis.

Code Representation

A tree structure where each node represents a construct in the source code (e.g., class, method, statement).

Static Analysis Engine

SonarQube's rules engine traverses the AST to identify code patterns or anti-patterns.

Custom Rule Interaction

When writing custom rules, you implement logic to traverse the AST and look for specific patterns.

Example: Java Code to AST
public class MyClass {
  public void myMethod() {
    int x = 10;
    if (x > 5) {
      System.out.println("Hello");
    }
  }
}
Key Takeaway

The AST transforms raw code into a structured, analyzable format, making complex static analysis possible for both built-in and custom rules.

screens.title: What is a SonarQube Plugin?
screens.narratorSegment: So, how do you actually introduce your custom rules into SonarQube? The answer lies in what's called a SonarQube plugin. Essentially, a SonarQube plugin is a standard Java Archive, or JAR, file. This JAR file isn't just a container for your custom rules; it can also include any necessary configurations, additional sensors for data collection, or other extensions that enhance SonarQube's capabilities. Think of it as a modular add-on that you can seamlessly integrate into your SonarQube server. Once developed and packaged, these plugins are deployed to a specific directory on your SonarQube server. After a quick restart, your custom rules become available for activation within your Quality Profiles, just like any of SonarQube's built-in rules. This modular approach ensures that SonarQube remains flexible and extensible, allowing you to tailor its behavior without modifying its core codebase. It's a powerful mechanism for administrators and architects to truly customize their code quality gates. screens.title: Writing Your Custom Rule Logic
screens.narratorSegment: Once your development environment is set up, the core task of custom rule development begins: implementing the rule logic itself. This is where you write the code that will traverse the Abstract Syntax Tree, or AST, and identify the specific issues you want to flag. SonarQube provides specialized APIs for different programming languages, such as SonarJava for Java, SonarJS for JavaScript, and SonarPython for Python. These APIs give you programmatic access to the AST nodes, allowing you to inspect the structure of the code. Your custom rule will typically extend a base visitor class, overriding methods like visit Method Invocation or visit Class to define what happens when the analyzer encounters specific code constructs. For example, if you want to check method calls, you'd implement logic within visit Method Invocation. This is a powerful mechanism, but it requires a deep understanding of both the language's syntax and the structure of its AST. A common pitfall here is not fully understanding the AST, leading to rules that either miss issues or generate false positives. Thoroughly understanding the AST for your target language is paramount for writing effective and accurate custom rules.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.2›Writing Your Custom Rule Logic

Writing Your Custom Rule Logic

Traversing the AST to identify specific code patterns.

AST Traversal

Implement logic to navigate the Abstract Syntax Tree, inspecting nodes and their relationships.

Language-Specific APIs

Utilize APIs like SonarJava, SonarJS, or SonarPython to access and manipulate AST nodes.

Issue Reporting

When a pattern is detected, the rule reports an issue with a descriptive message and location.

Conceptual Rule Structure
public class MyCustomRule extends BaseTreeVisitor {
  @Override
  public void visitMethodInvocation(MethodInvocationTree tree) {
    // Logic to inspect method calls
    if (isForbiddenMethod(tree)) {
      // context.reportIssue(this, tree, "Forbidden method call");
    }
    super.visitMethodInvocation(tree);
  }
  // ... other visit methods for different AST nodes
}
Key Takeaway

Writing custom rule logic involves extending a visitor class and implementing methods to inspect specific AST nodes for desired patterns.

screens.title: Packaging and Deploying Your Plugin
screens.narratorSegment: After you've meticulously crafted your custom rule logic, the next crucial step is to package and deploy your plugin. This process transforms your source code into a functional SonarQube extension that the server can understand and execute. Using Maven, which we set up earlier, you'll compile your Java code and package it into a standard JAR file. This JAR file is your complete plugin, ready for deployment. Once packaged, you simply copy this. jar file into the extensions slash plugins directory on your SonarQube server. It's important to note that after placing the file, you must restart your SonarQube server for it to discover and load the new plugin. Without a restart, the server won't recognize your custom rules. Finally, after the server is back online, you can navigate to the Administration section, specifically Quality Profiles, where your new custom rules will be listed and available for activation. You can then add them to your existing Quality Profiles, just like any built-in rule, and they will be applied in subsequent code analyses. This entire process ensures that your custom logic is seamlessly integrated into your SonarQube instance, ready to enforce your unique code quality standards.

screens.title: Conceptual AST Traversal for DB Access Rule
screens.narratorSegment: Let's dive into a conceptual code snippet to see how our 'No Direct DB Access' rule might work. This example uses SonarJava's A P I, which provides the tools to interact with the Java AST. Our custom rule class, No Direct Db Access Rule, extends Base Tree Visitor. This means it can visit different nodes in the AST. We'd override methods like visit Method Invocation to inspect method calls. Inside this method, we check if the invoked method is a known database access method, such as prepare Statement or create Query. If it is, we then need to determine the class from which this method call originates. We traverse up the AST from the method invocation to find its enclosing class. Once we have the class name, we simply check if it ends with our defined REPOSITORY underscore SUFFIX. If it doesn't, we've found a violation, and we report an issue. Similarly, we might override visit New Class to detect direct instantiations of database-related objects, like Connection or Driver Manager, applying the same logic to ensure they are within a 'Repository' class. This demonstrates the power of AST traversal: you're not just searching for text, but understanding the code's structure and context.

keyIdea.text: Custom rules traverse the AST using visitor methods to identify specific method calls or object instantiations and check their contextual compliance.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.2›Conceptual AST Traversal for DB Access Rule

Conceptual AST Traversal for DB Access Rule

Illustrating custom rule logic with a simplified Java code snippet.

visitMethodInvocation

Inspects method calls like prepareStatement or createQuery.

Contextual Check

Determines the enclosing class and verifies if its name ends with "Repository".

Issue Reporting

Flags an issue if direct DB access is found outside a *Repository class.

Simplified Java Rule Logic
public class NoDirectDbAccessRule extends BaseTreeVisitor {

    private static final String REPOSITORY_SUFFIX = "Repository";

    @Override
    public void visitMethodInvocation(MethodInvocationTree tree) {
        String methodName = tree.methodSelect().token().text();
        if (methodName.equals("prepareStatement") || methodName.equals("createQuery")) {
            Tree parentClass = tree.parent();
            while (parentClass != null && parentClass.kind() != Tree.Kind.CLASS) {
                parentClass = parentClass.parent();
            }
            if (parentClass != null) {
                String className = ((TypeTree) parentClass).simpleName().name();
                if (!className.endsWith(REPOSITORY_SUFFIX)) {
                    // Report an issue: "Direct DB access outside of a Repository class."
                    System.out.println("Issue found: Direct DB access outside of " + REPOSITORY_SUFFIX + " in class " + className);
                }
            }
        }
        super.visitMethodInvocation(tree);
    }
    // Similar logic for visitNewClass to detect direct DB object instantiation
}

Connection object, rather than just a variable named 'connection', makes your rule much more precise. Symbol analysis helps you understand the scope and definition of identifiers, preventing false positives by distinguishing between local variables and actual A P I calls. Without these advanced features, your rules might be prone to incorrect flags or might miss subtle issues. For example, a simple string match for 'connection' could flag a benign variable, but with type resolution, you can confirm it's a database connection object. screens.title: Avoiding Mistakes in Custom Rule Development
screens.narratorSegment: Developing custom rules for SonarQube is a powerful capability, but it comes with its own set of challenges. One of the most common mistakes is incorrect AST traversal. If your rule doesn't visit the right nodes or misses crucial edge cases, it can lead to either false positives, where valid code is flagged as an issue, or false negatives, where actual issues are overlooked. Another significant concern is performance. Inefficient rule logic can drastically slow down your SonarQube analysis, impacting your CI/CD pipeline. Thorough testing with a diverse set of code samples is absolutely essential to catch these issues early. Furthermore, a lack of proper error handling within your plugin can lead to crashes during SonarQube analysis, disrupting your entire quality gate. Remember, custom plugins introduce external code into your SonarQube instance. Always ensure that your plugins are sourced from trusted developers or developed internally with rigorous code reviews. Treat custom plugins with the same security scrutiny as any other third-party dependency in your production environment. By being aware of these common pitfalls, you can develop more reliable and effective custom rules.

At the heart of how SonarQube performs static analysis lies a fundamental concept: the Abstract Syntax Tree, or AST. Think of an AST as a hierarchical, tree-like representation of your source code, but stripped of all the syntactic details that aren't essential for understanding its structure. For example, when you write an 'if' statement, a 'for' loop, a method declaration, or a variable assignment in your code, each of these constructs is represented as a distinct node within the AST. SonarQube's powerful rules engine then traverses this tree, systematically examining each node and its relationships to others, searching for specific patterns or anti-patterns that indicate potential code quality issues or vulnerabilities. When you develop a custom rule, you are essentially writing your own code that also navigates this very same AST, allowing you to pinpoint and flag your organization's unique patterns. Understanding the AST is crucial because it's the canvas on which all SonarQube's analysis, both built-in and custom, is painted. So, how do you actually introduce your custom rules into SonarQube? The answer lies in what's called a SonarQube plugin. Essentially, a SonarQube plugin is a standard Java Archive, or JAR, file. Developing custom rules for SonarQube is a powerful capability, but it comes with its own set of challenges. One of the most common mistakes is incorrect AST traversal. If your rule doesn't visit the right nodes or misses crucial edge cases, it can lead to either false positives, where valid code is flagged as an issue, or false negatives, where actual issues are overlooked. Another significant concern is performance. Inefficient rule logic can drastically slow down your SonarQube analysis, impacting your CI/CD pipeline. Thorough testing with a diverse set of code samples is absolutely essential to catch these issues early. Furthermore, a lack of proper error handling within your plugin can lead to crashes during SonarQube analysis, disrupting your entire quality gate. Remember, custom plugins introduce external code into your SonarQube instance. Always ensure that your plugins are sourced from trusted developers or developed internally with rigorous code reviews. Treat custom plugins with the same security scrutiny as any other third-party dependency in your production environment. By being aware of these common pitfalls, you can develop more reliable and effective custom rules.
